tour.title: Stone Houses, Windmills & the Aegean
tour.summary: A slow late-afternoon walk through a Greek Orthodox village that became a Turkish one — stone houses, an old church turned mosque, the food street, and four windmills for sunset.
tour.overviewText:
Alaçatı looks like a village built for postcards and then forced to live in one. Bougainvillea climbs lilac-painted balconies, cobbled lanes thread between pale stone houses, and four windmills stand on a low hill above the roofs. The prettiness is real, but it is the second act. The first act is a Greek Orthodox village.

For roughly two centuries before 1923 this was Alatsata, a Greek-speaking, Greek Orthodox town of the Ottoman Empire — Rum, in Turkish, from "Roman", the word Turks used for the Orthodox Christians of the empire, heirs of Byzantium. In 1904 it had around fifteen thousand people, almost all of them Rum. Local tradition says the community began in the eighteenth century, when a regional notable, Hacı Memiş Ağa, brought families from Chios and the nearby islands to drain the malarial marsh that covered this ground. They drained it, farmed it, and built the stone houses you are about to walk between.

Then the ground shifted. After the Greco-Turkish war of 1919–22, Greece and Turkey agreed at Lausanne in 1923 to a compulsory exchange of populations, sorted not by language but by religion: about 1.2 million Greek Orthodox Christians left Turkey for Greece, and somewhere between 355,000 and 400,000 Muslims left Greece for Turkey. The Muslims who came to this village — from Kavala, Veria, Crete and Macedonia — moved into houses whose Greek owners had just been forced out. Neither community chose it; the two states did. Alaçatı's stone houses passed to Turkish families, and the village went quiet for the next seventy years.

What changed it again was taste. In the 2000s İzmir and Istanbul discovered the place: old houses were restored into boutique hotels and courtyards became restaurants. The state had already declared the old centre a protected historical site in 2005, which is why so much original stonework survived the boom instead of being bulldozed. Today about ten thousand people live here year-round, and the economy leans on visitors, vineyards and — above all — wind. The Çeşme peninsula funnels the meltemi, the dry northern Aegean wind, and the shallow bay south of town has become one of the world's best windsurfing and kitesurfing spots. Supporters call the transformation renewal; critics say the village has been priced and prettified out of its own life. Both arguments are standing in front of you.

The walk is short and gentle: a slow northward drift from the old square through the lanes and past the old church, out along the food street, and up to the windmills for sunset. The walking itself is barely a kilometre — the village is that compact — but with time spent at each stop it fills a slow late afternoon. It is flat apart from the last short rise, cobbled underfoot, and best started in the late afternoon, when the light turns the stone honey-coloured. Everything on the route is free to walk; only what you eat or buy costs money. Take it slowly, and look up as often as down — the balconies are the best part.
tour.difficulty: Easy. Flat cobbled lanes for most of the walk, with one short gentle climb up to the windmills on a paved path. Surfaces are uneven stone and cobble throughout, and the lanes are narrow — watch your footing, and expect restaurant tables and scooters to share the space with you.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Late afternoon into sunset. Start around 4 to 5pm so the lanes are still bright, the cafés are opening and you reach the windmills for the hour before sunset, when the stone turns gold and the meltemi usually eases. Mornings are quieter and cooler but the light over the roofs is flatter. If you are here on a Saturday, come for the market earlier and walk afterwards.

stops.name: Hacı Memiş Square
stops.narration:
You are in the old centre of the village, in the quarter the locals call Hacımemiş — the quieter, less-restored half of the old town. The small mosque beside the square is the Hacı Memiş Ağa Camii, an early nineteenth-century mosque built, local accounts say, in 1812, and named for an eighteenth-century notable of the region. Start with him, because he explains who lived here.

Hacı Memiş Ağa was a local strongman — an ayan, the kind of provincial notable who ran things on behalf of the Ottoman state. The story in these lanes is that he brought Greek families from Chios and the nearby islands to drain the malarial marsh that covered this ground. They did, and they stayed. By the nineteenth century this was a Greek Orthodox village: in 1904 it had around fifteen thousand people, almost all of them what Turks call Rum — the Greek Orthodox Christians of the Ottoman Empire, heirs of Byzantium, "Romans" in the old imperial sense.

The name is a puzzle with no single answer. Some trace it to the Greek word for salt, alati, through the older form Alatsata; Turkish records from 1525 give Alacat or Alacaat, from alaca at — a piebald or reddish horse. Either way, the village only settled on its present spelling in 1928.

Then came the rupture. After the Greco-Turkish war of 1919 to 1922, Greece and Turkey agreed at Lausanne in 1923 to a compulsory exchange of populations. It was sorted by religion, not language: around 1.2 million Greek Orthodox Christians left Turkey for Greece, and somewhere between 355,000 and 400,000 Muslims left Greece for Turkey. Exemptions were carved out — the Greeks of Istanbul and the Muslims of Western Thrace stayed — but almost everyone else went. The Muslims who arrived in this village came from Kavala, Veria, Crete and Macedonia, and they moved into houses whose Greek owners had just been forced out. Nobody here chose it; the two governments did. That is the plainest way to say it, and the fairest.

So the houses changed hands and the village went quiet — a farming and fishing town, then almost forgotten, for seventy years. Alaçatı is today a mahalle, a neighbourhood of the Çeşme district in İzmir province, with about ten and a half thousand residents. Look around the square: plane trees, tea glasses, old men, cats. This is the part of town that still belongs to the people who live here. Walk north now, into the lanes, and watch the houses.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. It is a public square, open at all hours. The mosque beside it is free to enter outside prayer times.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. The square is liveliest in the morning and again in the evening.
stops.accessibility: Level paved square, step-free across the middle, though the surrounding lanes are cobbled and uneven. Benches and café seating all around.
stops.insiderTip: This is the quieter, genuinely lived-in end of the old town — far less polished than Kemalpaşa Caddesi. Sit with a tea and watch the morning errands before you start walking; it is the best place to see that people still live here, not just visit.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the square on its north side and walk up into the lanes, keeping the minaret behind you. Follow any of the cobbled streets climbing gently north for about four hundred metres; they all funnel into the same tangle of stone houses. The next stop is simply the lanes themselves.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Fatih Demirci, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: The Stone-House Lanes
stops.narration:
Now read the walls. Almost everything here is built from a pale, porous stone — locally called ponza taşı, a volcanic tuff quarried on this peninsula. It is soft enough to cut when it comes out of the ground and hardens as it dries, and it is full of air pockets, which makes it light and a decent insulator. That is why these houses stay cool through an Aegean summer without air conditioning.

The signature detail is the cumba: an enclosed balcony or alcove window that juts out over the street on the upper floor. In an Alaçatı house the cumba is usually painted lilac or pale blue, and behind its glazing a family could sit and watch the lane without being watched back. The windows are often coloured too, which is the town's other trademark. Notice how high the garden walls are, and how the lanes bend and narrow: this was built for shade, for privacy, and to break the wind that never quite stops.

The houses are nineteenth-century, and they exist because the ground was drained. For centuries this was marsh, and marsh meant malaria; a canal dug in the 1850s — the Alataş — finally dried it out, and the town could grow. Greek and Turkish masons built side by side, using the same stone and much the same plan, which is why you cannot tell the two communities' houses apart at a glance — except by that projecting cumba.

Then fast-forward a century. By the 1990s Alaçatı was a sleepy place full of beautiful, crumbling houses. In the 2000s İzmir and Istanbul discovered it. Houses were bought, restored and turned into boutique hotels and courtyard restaurants, and the state had declared the old centre a protected historical site in 2005 — the reason so much original stonework survived the boom instead of being bulldozed. Walk a few lanes and you will see the result: a restored house is now a business — a nine-room hotel, a ceramics shop, a breakfast terrace.

That is the argument you can hear over dinner here. Supporters say restoration saved the houses; critics say the village was sold to weekenders and that in summer it belongs more to visitors than to residents. Both are true at once. What is not in doubt is the craftsmanship: run your hand along a wall and you are touching stone cut, hauled and laid by hand, by people who thought they were building for their grandchildren.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. These are public lanes; the houses are private homes and working hotels, so admire from the street and do not wander into courtyards uninvited.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Lanes are quietest in the morning; hotels and shops along them keep their own hours.
stops.accessibility: Uneven cobbles throughout, with low steps and drainage channels across some lanes. No step-free route through the old quarter — take it slowly and watch your footing.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the projecting enclosed balconies painted lilac or pale blue — that cumba is the giveaway of a Greek-built house. Photograph the doors and windows rather than the residents; these are people's front rooms, not exhibits.
stops.nextStopDirections: Keep climbing north through the lanes for another two or three minutes. The street opens slightly and the old church-turned-mosque — a long stone building with a minaret — stands on your right. That is the Pazaryeri Camii.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Justinianus, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Pazaryeri Camii
stops.narration:
Here is the exchange in stone. This building is the Pazaryeri Camii — the "marketplace mosque", so called because it stands beside the market. But it was not built as a mosque. It opened in 1874 as the Church of Ayios Konstantinos — Saint Constantine, the Roman emperor who legalised Christianity — begun in the 1830s by a local Greek benefactor named Yuhannis Halapes. It is a three-nave basilica in rubble stone, and it was one of three large churches the Rum community built for itself. It is the only one still standing.

Look at the bones of it: the long rectangular hall, the columns dividing the interior into three aisles, the rounded apse end. A basilica is a Roman hall plan that early Christians adopted for churches, and it is unmistakable once you know it. Then look at what has been added since — the mihrab, the niche that points the congregation toward Mecca, the minaret, the carpet. A mosque now occupies a church's skeleton. That is not unusual in Turkey; what makes this one worth a stop is that the change happened within living memory of the village.

Here is how the 1923 exchange actually worked, because it is easy to misstate. Greece and Turkey sorted people by faith, not by language or ancestry. A Greek Orthodox Christian who spoke only Turkish — there were many, in Cappadocia — was sent to Greece. A Muslim who spoke only Greek — there were many too, in Crete — was sent to Turkey. The deal exempted the Greek Orthodox of Istanbul and the Muslims of Western Thrace. Almost everyone else in the two countries was, in effect, traded. This church became a mosque because its congregation was gone and a new Muslim congregation had arrived to take its place.

Behave as you would in any working mosque: shoes off at the door, shoulders and knees covered, voices low, and women are usually offered a headscarf. Entry is free — there is no ticket — and donations for upkeep are welcome but never required. It closes to visitors during the five daily prayers, and prayer times shift through the year, so if the door is shut, wait or come back: this is somebody's place of worship first and a monument second.

When you leave, turn north again. Two minutes up the lane is the street where the town eats.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. It is a working mosque, not a ticketed site. Donations for upkeep are welcome but never required.
stops.openingHours: Open to visitors outside the five daily prayer times; closed during prayers and for the Friday midday congregation. Prayer times shift daily — if the door is shut, wait a little or come back.
stops.accessibility: A step or two at the entrance, then a level carpeted floor inside. The old basilica has columns and thresholds to mind.
stops.insiderTip: Stand at the back and look down the length of the hall: the three-aisle basilica plan is still perfectly readable under the mosque fittings. It is the clearest single piece of evidence in the village that this was a Greek town.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the mosque, turn north and walk two minutes up the lane until it meets the main shopping street, where the tables and shopfronts begin. That is Kemalpaşa Caddesi — the next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Eudessa, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Kemalpaşa Caddesi & the Saturday Market
stops.narration:
Kemalpaşa Caddesi is the town's main street, named, like a thousand streets in Turkey, after Mustafa Kemal Paşa — Atatürk, the founder of the modern republic. In the last twenty years it has become Alaçatı's stage: boutiques, wine bars and restaurant tables spilling across the cobbles until you can barely squeeze past. It is the busiest and most photographed lane in the village, and by evening it is one long dinner party.

What it is really about is food, and Alaçatı's food is built on wild greens. In Turkish they are simply ot — "herb" — and along this coast they are gathered in spring from the fields and hillsides: nettles, wild fennel, purslane, mallow, sorrel, and dozens more with no English name. Cooked with olive oil, eaten warm or cold with yoghurt and good bread, they are the backbone of an Aegean table. Every spring the town holds the Alaçatı Herb Festival — the Ot Festival — with foraging walks, tastings and cooking competitions; it is free to wander, and it has now run for more than a decade. Ask for "ot" on any menu and you will get whatever the season offered that morning.

The rest of the local canon is worth knowing. Kahvaltı is the Turkish breakfast — a spread of cheeses, olives, tomatoes, cucumber, honey, jams and endless tea — and Alaçatı has turned it into a weekend ritual. Kumru is İzmir's sandwich: a warm roll with cheese, tomato and sucuk, the garlicky fermented beef sausage. And then there is sakız, mastic, the resin of the mastic tree, Pistacia lentiscus, which grows across the strait on Chios and here on the Çeşme peninsula. Chewed, it softens and turns white; in the kitchen it flavours ice cream, pudding and even coffee. You will find it sold everywhere as sweets and soap.

If you are here on a Saturday, the real market is the thing. Alaçatı Pazarı has set up every Saturday since 1994 on 13000. Sokak and the streets around Cumhuriyet Caddesi, a few minutes' walk south of here — stalls of vegetables, herbs, cheese, olives, honey, textiles and handmade trinkets, roughly eight in the morning until seven or eight at night. It is famous enough that day-trippers come over from the Greek island of Chios, an hour by ferry, just for it. Prices are whatever the seller says; carry some cash, because small notes make life easier than cards at a stall.

So eat, buy, and read the price tags. This street is where the transformation of the village is most visible: the money that restored the stone houses comes, in large part, from the tables you are standing between. Whether that is a rescue or a takeover is the question the town is still arguing about.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk. Food, drink and shopping are at menu and stall prices — verify before you order, and carry cash in small notes for the market.
stops.openingHours: Street shops and cafés typically run daily from mid-morning until late evening. The Saturday market sets up roughly 08:00 to 19:00–20:00 on Saturdays only — confirm on the day, as it is a municipal market and times can shift.
stops.accessibility: Cobbled and mostly level, but narrow: tables, chairs and crowds can block the pavement, and there are occasional steps at shop entrances. Manageable with care, not step-free in the busiest hours.
stops.insiderTip: Order ot — the wild greens of the season — and ask what is in it; it changes week to week. If it is Saturday, walk south to 13000. Sokak for the produce market rather than buying from the tourist shops here.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north up Kemalpaşa Caddesi and, where it ends, follow Uğur Mumcu Caddesi as it climbs gently toward the hill. In about two hundred metres the four windmills come into view on the knoll ahead — the last stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Bir_Ege_Hikayesi ©, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: The Windmills (Yel Değirmenleri)
stops.narration:
Climb the last few metres and turn around. From this low knoll you can see the whole village — stone roofs, the minaret, the sea beyond — and beside you stand four windmills, the emblem of Alaçatı. They are yel değirmenleri: yel is wind, değirmen is mill. These are nineteenth-century mills, most estimates dating them between about 1850 and 1920, and they are built in the shape Mediterranean windmills share — a cylindrical tower of rubble stone, two or three storeys high, once topped by a wooden cap carrying sails and a shaft that turned a millstone. Farmers brought wheat and barley up here and went home with flour. The sails are long gone and the machinery no longer turns; what you see has been restored and tidied in recent decades. But the reason they stand exactly here has not changed at all.

Which is the wind. This coast is one of the windiest corners of the Aegean, and it has a name for the wind: the meltemi — in Turkish meltem, probably borrowed from the Italian mal tempo, "bad weather". Meteorologists call the same winds the etesians, from the Greek word for "yearly", because they arrive like clockwork from about mid-May to mid-September. They are dry, strong northerlies that build through the afternoon and often drop at night; sailors treat them with respect, because they can rise out of a clear sky and blow at force seven or eight on the Beaufort scale. The Çeşme peninsula funnels them: the hills squeeze the airflow and the village sits in the channel. That is why the mills are here — and it is why the modern town has a second life.

Follow the wind south in your mind and you reach the bay, where the water is shallow and the breeze is steady: near-perfect conditions for windsurfing and kitesurfing, and the reason Alaçatı hosts world tour events and gets nicknamed, by people who enjoy that sort of thing, the slalom capital of the world. Schools line the shore; the Turkish windsurfing champion Çağla Kubat is from here. If the wind dropped while you were visiting and the boards stayed on the racks, you were unlucky — or, depending on your taste, lucky.

Two easy trips finish the picture. South, about nine kilometres, is Çeşme, the peninsula's old port town, with a castle the Genoese began and the Ottomans rebuilt in 1508 under Sultan Bayezid II; it now houses the Çeşme Museum, open daily in daylight hours, with a ticket that was around 100 ₺ in 2023 and has risen since — verify at the gate, as prices here move fast. North is Ilıca, whose name means "spa" and whose beach sits on geothermal springs; Çeşme itself means "fountain". A dolmuş — a shared minibus — runs between the village and both; pay the driver in cash.

Now stay put. This is the best place in Alaçatı to watch the sun go down: the stone turns honey, the wind usually eases, and the terraces light up one at a time. You have just walked through two centuries of it — a Greek village, a Turkish village, and now a place that half-lives on visitors. The windmills have watched all three. When you are ready, the lanes back down take three or four minutes, and dinner is waiting.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. It is an open hilltop with no ticket and no gate; the mills are historic structures, not a paid attraction.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Best in the hour before sunset; after dark the path is unlit, so bring a phone light for the walk down.
stops.accessibility: A short paved climb from the lane, then an uneven stone-and-grass knoll around the mills. Not step-free; the path is manageable but slopes and the ground is rough underfoot.
stops.insiderTip: Come for the last hour of light and stay ten minutes past sunset — the wind often drops in the evening and the village below goes gold, then the terraces switch on. It is the best free view in town.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Stay for sunset if you can, then follow the paved path back down the knoll and retrace Uğur Mumcu Caddesi into the village — three or four minutes back down to the lanes and the dinner tables of Kemalpaşa Caddesi. For Çeşme and its castle, a dolmuş or taxi from the centre takes about fifteen minutes; for Ilıca beach, the same in the other direction. Both are worth a half-day before you leave.
